reason: Gives a usable sorting test: what would an attacker have to get past? Logic in software or hardware covers the firewall and encryption. A person's judgement or an organisational decision covers the AUP and background check. Something solid covers the door and fence. Each item maps cleanly to one bucket and nothing points the wrong way.

Names the main trap: classifying by the asset protected, so the AUP and background checks land under Technical because they protect IT systems. It overlaps with hint 0 on 'classify by the enforcer', but adds the asset-versus-enforcer distinction that fixes that specific mistake.

The 'flip it' test steers the qualification item wrong. Its opposite is taking on work you can't deliver while implying you can, which reads as breaking the 'personal rule against deceit', so the learner picks Canon II. The exam convention puts competence under Canon III, and since no engagement exists yet ('up front'), the 'commitment built into your engagement' option doesn't feel like it applies. Flipping the mentoring item breaks nothing in particular, so the test gives no answer there and the learner is left guessing by elimination.

Heads off the likely mistake of starting with Assess because the vulnerability is already known. The learner has to ask what must be known before likelihood and impact can be judged, which puts Identify asset/threats/vulnerabilities first. It is accurate and does not overlap with hint 1, which covers the end of the sequence.

Gives a dependency test for the tail of the sequence: risk only drops once a control is applied and verified, and residual risk can only be documented after that. This puts Apply/verify before Document residual, which is correct. Hint 0 doesn't cover this.

It says all internal documents form one chain, each carrying out the one above. Guidelines are not in that mandatory chain: they are non-binding advice that sits alongside it. So the hint invites placing the passphrase item as a Standard or Procedure. The 'carries out the one above' test also suggests 'Every system must have a named owner' carries out the customer-data confidentiality policy, which pushes that policy-level responsibility statement into Standard. What it does add is mostly hint 0's specificity question again, without the binding-versus-advised test that actually separates out the Guideline item.
